drug_class: Antiretroviral – HIV Protease Inhibitor (also used as a pharmacokinetic booster)
purpose: Ritonavir is used to help treat HIV, the virus that can lead to AIDS. It is most commonly used in combination with other HIV medications to help keep the virus under control. It can also be used in low doses to boost the levels of other HIV drugs in your body, making them work better.
how_it_works: HIV needs a special tool called a protease enzyme to make copies of itself inside your body. Ritonavir blocks that tool, so the virus cannot finish building new copies of itself. This helps lower the amount of HIV in your blood and keeps your immune system stronger. At low doses, it also slows down the breakdown of other HIV medicines so they stay in your body longer and work more effectively.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach pain are the most common issues, especially when you first start taking it. You may also notice tingling or numbness around your mouth, a change in taste, tiredness, or headache. Some people experience increased cholesterol or blood sugar levels over time.
warnings: Ritonavir interacts with a very large number of other medications — including some common ones — so always tell every doctor and pharmacist exactly what you are taking. It can cause serious heart rhythm problems if combined with certain drugs. People with liver problems need to be monitored closely. Never stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, as stopping can allow HIV to become harder to treat.
typical_dosing: For HIV treatment, the usual adult dose is 600 mg twice a day, taken with food to help reduce stomach upset. When used as a booster for other HIV medicines, the dose is much lower — typically 100 mg once or twice a day. Your doctor will set the exact dose that is right for your specific treatment plan.
